title: An-Nazi'at: those who pull out
hook: by the angels who draw out souls gently and harshly (79:1–2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of 'Abasa, a day when each person flees even their own family. Your line was each alone that day. Who did you hold close? Day two hundred sixteen.

If you've ever sat with someone at the end of their life, you may remember the breathing most. Long pauses. The room holding still. And then the moment when a breath goes out and doesn't come back in. People who've been there often say it was quieter than they expected, and sometimes, strangely, peaceful. Every tradition has had to find words for that moment. The surah just before 'Abasa opens with its own words for it, in a pair of oaths that are hard to translate and have been read several ways. Today: An-Nazi'at, those who pull out.
screen: `THE LAST BREATH IN A QUIET ROOM.` → `QUIETER THAN EXPECTED.` → `AN-NAZI'AT, THOSE WHO PULL OUT.`

segments.voice: Surah seventy-nine begins with an oath: by those who pull out, forcefully. Then: by those who draw out, gently. The first word, an-nazi'at, is from a root meaning to pull, to wrench something out. The second, an-nashitat, has a softer picture behind it: loosening a knot, or easing a bucket up out of a well. The surah doesn't say who these are. Most commentators say they are angels, the ones who take souls at death. From some, the soul is pulled out hard. From others, it is drawn out gently. Other early commentators read the oaths as stars moving across the sky, or as death itself, or as arrows drawn from a bow. The text leaves it open, and the scholars have left it open too. But the angels reading is the one most Muslims know, and a long hadith, reported in Abu Dawud and in Ahmad's collection, fills it in. It says that when a believer dies, the soul leaves as easily as a drop of water flows from the mouth of a waterskin. And for others, it is dragged like a skewer through wet wool. Hard to hear. But notice which picture the surah puts second, closest to what follows: gently. Many Muslims pray for exactly this, an easy departure, and ask at the bedsides of the dying for the soul to be drawn out gently. And death here isn't a stranger crashing in. It's a door that's been attended to. Someone is sent. Someone does the drawing out. Nobody leaves unaccompanied.
screen: `AN-NAZI'AT — PULLED OUT HARD.` · `AN-NASHITAT — A KNOT LOOSENED.` · `ANGELS, STARS, OR DEATH ITSELF.` · `NOBODY LEAVES UNACCOMPANIED.` · then, large: `GENTLY DRAWN.`

segments.voice: For two minutes, just watch your breath going out. Not in. Out. Let each exhale be slow and complete, like water poured from a jug until it's empty. Notice the small pause at the bottom before the next breath comes on its own. Nothing to fix. Just the out-breath, gently drawn, and the one that comes after. The bell holds the time.
An-Nazi'at. Those who pull out, the opening word of Surah seventy-nine, paired with those who draw out gently. Today's word.
Your line: gently drawn. Once today, when you're tense, let one long breath out, slowly, all the way to the bottom. Day two hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Muslims believe angels take each soul at death; many pray for an easy passing, and at a deathbed family often recite the shahada gently and read Qur'an, hoping the soul is drawn out with ease.

fork.setup: An-Nazi'at swears by 'those who pull out' and 'those who draw out gently'. who do most commentators say they are?
fork.reveal: most say the angels who take souls at death; others read stars, death itself, or arrows. the text leaves it open.

original.note: Arabic: "those who pull out," from n-z-', to pull or wrench out; the name of Surah 79.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah that starts with something scary.
what it means: oaths by those who draw souls out, some hard, some gently, read by most as the angels at death.

what a scholar hears: gharqan, drowning deep, qualifies the first oath; the angels reading goes back to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas in al-Tabari; the waterskin image is from the long hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.

sources.ref: Qur'an 79:1–5 (those who pull out, those who draw out gently, those who glide, race, and arrange)
Sunan Abi Dawud 4753; Musnad Ahmad (the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib on the soul's departure)

notes: All Qur'an text paraphrased today (not certain enough of Pickthall's rendering of 79:1–2).
The al-Bara' hadith: Abu Dawud 4753 is an abridged version; the full text with the waterskin and wet wool images is in Musnad Ahmad. Confirm numbers and wording.
Attributions of readings in al-Tabari (Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas) cited from memory; confirm.
Deathbed practice in howItsDone (reciting the shahada, reading Yasin) varies; stated generally.
